taxonomy.subsystem: Bone extracellular matrix and collagen genetics
taxonomy.subtopic: COL1A1 haploinsufficiency versus dominant-negative type I collagen defects

questions.stem_html: An 8-year-old girl has sustained four long-bone fractures after minor falls. Examination shows blue-gray sclerae and mild joint laxity. Her father had similar childhood fractures but has normal height. Genetic testing identifies a premature termination variant in one COL1A1 allele. The accompanying diagram compares two mechanisms of type I collagen disease. Which molecular consequence is most likely in this child?

options.text_html: Production of approximately half the normal amount of structurally normal type I collagen
Secretion of abnormal type I collagen that incorporates into and destabilizes most triple helices
Failure to hydroxylate lysine residues because of deficient vitamin C
Replacement of type I collagen by type II collagen in cortical bone
Excess osteoclast differentiation caused by constitutive RANK activation

questions.explanation_html: A premature termination variant in one COL1A1 allele commonly causes nonsense-mediated decay and haploinsufficiency. The result is reduced quantity of otherwise structurally normal type I collagen, a mechanism associated with the milder, nondeforming form of osteogenesis imperfecta. By contrast, glycine substitutions in the triple-helical domain can produce abnormal chains that enter collagen trimers and exert a dominant-negative effect, often causing more severe disease.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: A structurally abnormal alpha chain can poison collagen trimers through a dominant-negative effect, but that mechanism is more typical of glycine substitutions and generally produces a more severe phenotype than a null allele.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Vitamin C deficiency impairs proline and lysine hydroxylation and causes scurvy; it is acquired and does not explain an autosomal dominant family pattern with a COL1A1 stop variant.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Type II collagen is the principal collagen of cartilage and vitreous, not a compensatory replacement for type I collagen in bone.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Constitutive RANK signaling would increase osteoclast activity but would not explain blue sclerae or a COL1A1 pathogenic variant.

questions.educational_objective: COL1A1 loss-of-function variants can cause haploinsufficiency with reduced production of structurally normal type I collagen, whereas structural variants may act through dominant-negative incorporation into collagen trimers.

media.alt_text: Original diagram contrasting COL1A1 haploinsufficiency, which reduces the quantity of normal collagen, with a dominant-negative structural collagen defect.
